doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Clare Fischer's Portrait of Duke Ellington and Extension
summary: Fischer's unusual instrumentation and the Extension record; Dobbins's piano background and Pentecostal father.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: sounded as modern as anything anybody was doing, but first of all they always sounded like jazz because they had the jazz beat. And then they also sounded like jazz because they also had this incredible mixture of the chromatic tonal harmony that you hear in European music from around the time of Bach through at least the Russian composers who still had ties with tonality whether it was in an obvious way like with Rachmaninoff or a less obvious way like with Shostakovich and Prokofiev or early Stravinsky, there was still a definite tie with tonality that was colored and filtered but it still was in the key and you could still hear it when you were on the way somewhere and then you would arrive there, you know. And so to me that’s a great correspondence to this idea in Wilber’s book of transcending and including. And the same thing with somebody like Clare Fischer. You hear, he could play, well yeah, there’s a blues that he wrote, this is another good example of the so-called wrong note stuff too, but you can find this stuff in Ellington and Strayhorn’s work, and Brookmeyer, any of the best jazz composers. I bought this record of Clare’s when I was in high school. It came out in ’63. It was called “Extension.” He did a record for Dizzy Gillespie around 1960 or ’61 called “Portrait of Duke Ellington” where he experimented with a different kind of big band. It was a big band with no trumpets. And I’m not sure if he didn’t use trumpets because Dizzy was going to be the soloist, or if it was just a novel reason. But it was saxophones with lots of woodwinds, from flute down to bass clarinet, and the brass section instead of trombones and trumpets it was three French horns, one trombone, one bass trombone and one tuba. It was the six brass, and then piano, bass and drums. Well a couple of years later he put out this record on the Pacific label called “Extension.” And it was a similar instrumentation only there was sometimes six saxophones in some of the pieces, and he added an organ. Instead of using it like a Jimmy Smith kind of jazz organ thing, he actually used it like an extra reed section. And then vibes as well as piano and organ. And it’s one of the most amazing recordings of original jazz compositions that I’ve heard that were really connected to the traditions. This main title tune, “Extensions,” there is two themes. The first one is a blues. When I first got this record, in ’63, I mean my early background is classical piano lessons from the time I was nine through the end of my master’s degree. And I discovered jazz — this is another thing — I discovered jazz totally by accident. I was at a friend’s house in high school. My father was a Pentecostal minister so he didn’t want me anywhere near jazz. So when I was in high school I couldn’t be in the jazz band but I could accompany the chorus. So there was this guy in the chorus that — we used to hang out after school — and his father was a jazz fan. And this is interesting too, because this guy was not a musician per se. I mean he could read music to a certain extent, but he was not a virtuoso pianist.
